You pass things on, and you do it while changing the form to fit the room. The way a family does a holiday, a crew runs a job, a team closes a week — you carry the point of it, drop the trimmings, and people take the version from you. You can do this because the form stays under the meaning. Something is settled underneath, so the surface can move without the thing coming apart.
The adjusting as you go is the part worth keeping. Pick the group where your version of the practice is holding and has drifted from what it was — a routine, a phrase, a standing arrangement. Find one piece that stopped earning its place and retire it. Keep the rest. The balance costs a small correction every few weeks, not a lurch, and it stays yours to make.
1.sheetLine: You pass on the point, not the wrapping.

2.tense: You will spend the next season defending how the form has always been done, and the people you're teaching will start slipping out the side door.
2.verb: carrying what works forward
2.place: in the fog with enough light for one step
2.ask: Pick one rule you enforce in a group you lead, and let one round of it go unenforced — then watch what actually breaks.
2.core:
Already, before the meeting, you are braced at the version you'll insist on. The form of the practice has become the whole of it, and anyone who does it differently is wrong rather than just different. What you're holding so tightly was once a living answer to something. Now it's a fence, and the windows in it are sealed.
Stop holding up the part that isn't keeping anyone. Pick a rule you've been enforcing — a way of doing something, a phrase others are expected to use — and let one round of it pass unenforced. Watch what actually breaks. Most of it won't. Underneath, the point of the practice is intact, and you can take it up with both hands once the scaffolding comes away.
2.sheetLine: The letter has taken the place of the living thing.

3.tense: You stood at the door of a room full of people and never quite walked in, and no shared form has your name on it now.
3.verb: carrying what works forward
3.place: in the fog with enough light for one step
3.ask: For a few days, take something you keep working out from scratch, and sketch how it fits together on a page — then leave the page alone.
3.core:
No practice is holding you. The ones near you seem to be inside something — a faith, a craft, a family way — and you're outside it, smart and self-made and alone with that. You work the same things out fresh each time because nothing carries them for you between rounds. The door isn't as shut as it looks; the furniture inside was made by people too.
Don't reach for the feeling of belonging yet. Instead, take the thing you keep re-deriving for yourself — how you run a project, say, or how you hold a friendship — and step back far enough to sketch how it fits together on a page. Name the pattern in one line. Leave the line alone. What shows up is a form you've been carrying without anything to pass it through.
3.sheetLine: You keep reinventing what other hands once carried.

4.tense: You are already teaching something by the way you live in it, and the record in your own head says you're just getting by.
4.verb: carrying what works forward
4.place: in the fog with enough light for one step
4.ask: When someone copies how you do something, add or drop one small piece of it next time, and see what shifts in them.
4.core:
People copy what you do. A habit you run without thinking, a way of talking through a problem, a small ritual around work or food or endings — someone younger or newer or quieter is taking it in. You file it all as just getting by. The transmission is happening anyway, through your hands, and you aren't at the desk as its author.
You don't have to announce anything. The next time someone watches you do something and then does it their own way, that's the thing moving. Take a small piece of how you do it — the timing, the wording, the order — and adjust it one notch. Then see what the notch changed in them. The difference is usually small, and usually lands. Knowing you are the one putting it there is the whole work.
4.sheetLine: You're already handing it down. You just don't sign it.

1.tense: You are handing something on right now, and you are adjusting it as you go.
1.verb: carrying forward what has proven worth keeping, and letting it change hands
1.place: the place where what you are becomes visible by being lived
1.ask: Whatever you pass along — a phrase, a small way of doing something — change a little of it this week and then stop. Leave it alone for a few days and see what holds.
1.core:
What gets handed through you stays intact at the center and shifts at the edges. You keep the frame and move the one small piece that no longer fits, and that's why people take it from you without feeling handled. The meaning stays whole while the wording moves. Someone can join it without turning into a copy of you, and you can tell on the day it's working.

Equilibrium here isn't standing still. It's sensing where a little more belongs and where a little comes out, and standing calm is what lets two versions sit side by side without picking one. So make just the small correction — a word, a practice, changed a little, then left alone. What happens next tells you whether the rest still holds. Either way you'll be working with the real thing rather than a description of it.
1.sheetLine: Keep the frame, move the one piece that no longer fits.

2.tense: The way you keep what you value is starting to demand that everyone keep it the same way.
2.verb: carrying forward what has proven worth keeping, and letting it change hands
2.place: the place where what you are becomes visible by being lived
2.ask: Let a small form drop for a week — a set phrase, a fixed order, a rule about how it should be done. Don't defend it and don't rebuild it yet.
2.core:
What you hold dear has stopped bending, and the bending was how it stayed yours. You keep the form exact, and the exactness is doing the work that care used to do. People feel it as a requirement, and what they bring gets measured before it gets heard. You have sealed the windows that used to let the air in, and you are guarding a house nobody can enter.

One piece can come down without taking what you need with it. So let a small form lapse for a week: a set phrase, a fixed order, the way it has been done. Don't defend it, don't replace it yet. What falls was propped up. Stand in the space it leaves and notice what is actually carrying weight. Nothing is asked of you after that — the watching is enough, and it's where the next move comes from.
2.sheetLine: The exactness is doing the work that care used to do.

3.tense: You have been building your own way of seeing things, mostly alone, and it can feel like starting over.
3.verb: carrying forward what has proven worth keeping, and letting it change hands
3.place: the place where what you are becomes visible by being lived
3.ask: Look at the last few times you figured something out on your own. Set them side by side and find the move you keep making. Change nothing — just see the shape.
3.core:
You have been making your own way through things, and it costs you the sense that anyone else is walking it too. Every problem gets solved from the beginning. Nothing you arrive at gets handed to you, and nothing you arrive at gets handed on. The intelligence is real. It just has no company, and no ground under it that someone else laid first.

But there is a pattern in how you do it, and seeing it is not effort — it is the opposite. Step back and look at the last few times you worked something out alone. Same move, probably, each time. See how it works underneath, apart from one instance. Name it in a line and change nothing. Seen clearly enough, your own method becomes something you can stand on and, later, hand to somebody.
3.sheetLine: Every problem gets solved from the beginning, and nothing gets handed on.

4.tense: Someone is already taking something from you and keeping it, and you have not counted it as yours.
4.verb: carrying forward what has proven worth keeping, and letting it change hands
4.place: the place where what you are becomes visible by being lived
4.ask: Bring to mind a person who has picked something up from you. Let yourself know, quietly and without ceremony, that it came from you. That's all for now.
4.core:
People watch how you live and take something from it. You have been calling that ordinary, or nothing at all. Meanwhile what you do quietly gets repeated somewhere you can't see it, in words you didn't say. The teaching is already underway. The claim is what's missing, so the credit drifts to whoever happens to be standing nearby.

You don't have to take up a title or start explaining yourself. Just hold one center steady: a person, a thing they picked up from you, named plainly as yours, while everything else keeps moving. If it feels like boasting, that's the old reflex talking. Naming what you gave isn't a claim about your worth — it's accuracy, and it makes the next thing you pass on easier to give.
4.sheetLine: The teaching is already underway. The claim is missing.

1.tense: You are passing something on right now and the form of it is still yours to move.
1.verb: handing a meaning forward
1.place: seeing the whole pattern
1.ask: This week take something you hand on often. Find what has to stay in it, hold that steady, and change one other word around it.
1.core:
You hand a meaning forward and the way you hand it keeps shifting — a word swapped, a step loosened so someone unlike you can still walk in. The whole pattern is visible while you stand inside it, so what travels doesn't have to be frozen to stay true. Held this way, people belong without having to agree, and the meaning outlives its own wording.

Find what has to stay in the thing you pass on — the part that holds steady while everything around it moves — change one other word, and leave the change alone after that. That centre wasn't yours to guard. You get to teach, and the teaching gets to stay alive in your hands.
1.sheetLine: You can hand a meaning on and still let it move.

2.tense: By next season you will be defending the old form as if the form were the meaning itself.
2.verb: handing a meaning forward
2.place: seeing the whole pattern
2.ask: Name a rule around what you pass on that you keep from habit rather than conviction, and stop propping it — no announcement, just no longer held up.
2.core:
Where you hand a meaning forward, you've started bracing — insisting the old form is the meaning rather than its wrapping, and asking for agreement you once didn't need. Every window gets sealed at the edges, and what was meant to travel stands still. The pattern is still visible to you; you're refusing to let it breathe. Tightness this strong usually guards something loved, and it costs what the meaning was for.

Find a rule around how you pass this on that you keep up out of habit rather than because it's true. Stop propping it, quietly, with nothing said about why. What couldn't hold will come down; what was the real thing will still stand. The teaching gets lighter, and you get to hear the room again.
2.sheetLine: You are holding up the form and calling it the meaning.

3.tense: You have been working things out alone, and the framework you carry has nothing around it to hand to.
3.verb: handing a meaning forward
3.place: seeing the whole pattern
3.ask: Put the last three things you worked out into one shape — the move they share, no details — and stop once it's written.
3.core:
You see how things work underneath, and you do it from outside any shared framework, so each generation around you reinvents what you worked out years back. What you understand, you understand alone. The pattern stays in your hands and doesn't leave them, and the little that gets handed on walks out uncredited. Seeing the whole shape is here in you. Lately it stands at the door.

Put the last three things you figured out or said into one line — the move you keep making, none of the details. Not to fix anything; write it and stop. That line is the part of teaching that comes before words get chosen, and writing it down puts the shape where you can see that it's yours.
3.sheetLine: You see the shape of everything and keep it to yourself.

4.tense: You are handing something on while the story you tell has you standing on the side.
4.verb: handing a meaning forward
4.place: seeing the whole pattern
4.ask: Next time a person brings you a muddle, set the old way and your own way side by side, and don't pick for them.
4.core:
Something goes out through you and you have your back to it. You explain how a thing works, or you show someone the move they were missing, and you file it as filling time — nothing, obviously nothing. You see the whole pattern, so what you say next tends to be what someone needed, and you don't count it as having handed anything to anyone. The one who does it doesn't know.

Let both the old way and your own way sit in front of someone, side by side, and don't choose for them. Blending is what you do already and have filed as nothing. The meaning moves through you either way; naming it is only the light going on where the work has been happening.
4.sheetLine: You are already the one handing it on.

1.tense: You are handing on what matters while it is still alive, and it changes as it moves.
1.verb: Carrying what has proven worth keeping into what comes next
1.place: At the point where something is finished and can now be let go
1.ask: Take a recipe, a story, or a way the holidays go, and change one piece of it this time — a small piece. Notice what the change does to the rest.
1.core:
You pass things on and the passing doesn't freeze them. A recipe gets adjusted for who's at the table, a story gets told the way this year's listener needs it, and the thing survives because it moved. You can hold a room and a history at once, and what comes out the other side still holds the shape of where it came from.

That's why adjusting one piece isn't a betrayal. Change one part of something you carry — how it's worded, the order, the ingredients — and watch what shifts around it. Keeping a thing alive takes small corrections, made on purpose, and you're free to make them on purpose. What you're holding is sturdier than the version that stands still.
1.sheetLine: What you pass on stays alive because you let it change.

2.tense: You will be guarding the exact form of something while the people it was for have moved on.
2.verb: Carrying what has proven worth keeping into what comes next
2.place: At the point where something is finished and can now be let go
2.ask: Pick a rule you keep enforcing that no longer fits the people it's for. This week, stop propping it up — no announcement, no replacement. See what stays standing without it.
2.core:
There's a version of holding on where the form outranks the point. The words get said exactly right and mean less, the way it's been done becomes the reason it's done, and the windows are shut to keep the air in. The strain of keeping it up is the tell. What you're protecting has already stopped being what it protected.

So let one of those rules fall. Not a scene, not a statement — just stop holding it up, and watch. What's real in the thing will still be there without the enforcement. What comes down was being held by you, not by them, and the ground it clears is yours to stand on.
2.sheetLine: You're holding up a form that stopped holding anything.

3.tense: You have been building from nothing each time, as if no one had built any of this before you.
3.verb: Carrying what has proven worth keeping into what comes next
3.place: At the point where something is finished and can now be let go
3.ask: Look at three times you worked something out the hard way. Lay them side by side and find the one thing they share. Put that line somewhere you'll see it. Nothing else changes yet.
3.core:
The thread that carries things forward isn't reaching you, so every problem gets solved alone and every method gets invented again. It's efficient in a way that costs — nobody's work arrives at your hands, and yours arrives at no one's. You can see the shape of a problem clearly. What's missing is a line running through the times you've done it.

Before you build the next thing, look at the last few. Three of them, side by side, and what they share. That's not a system and you don't have to adopt it — it's the pattern your own work has been making without you, and it was already yours.
3.sheetLine: You keep reinventing a wheel you already own.

4.tense: Someone nearby is picking up how to do this from watching you, and you have not counted yourself as the source.
4.verb: Carrying what has proven worth keeping into what comes next
4.place: At the point where something is finished and can now be let go
4.ask: Choose something you do well that someone close to you has started doing too. Hold it as true without arguing it down, and do the thing the way you do it.
4.core:
You're already handing something on. Not in a class, not on purpose — someone close to you cooks it like you cook it, handles it the way you handle it, says it the way you say it, and it started with your hands. Asked about it, you'd say you weren't teaching anything. The teaching is happening anyway.

Nothing needs to change about what you do. Just hold the middle of it more deliberately — the way you stand when you're doing it well, steady, in the middle of the work — and make that the thing that gets copied. You're not taking a podium. You're noticing the one you've been standing on, and standing on it on purpose.
4.sheetLine: You've been the source of something you left unclaimed.
